Clean Skin Starts With the Right Bar

Meet Real Skin Care's Natural Coconut Oil Bar Soap — just four honest ingredients, nothing hidden.

Add to Cart

Updated April 2026 | By the Real Skin Care Editorial Team

A natural soap bar is a cleansing bar made through saponification — a chemical reaction between plant-based oils and an alkali — that produces real soap, retained glycerin, and none of the petroleum-derived surfactants found in most commercial bars. That distinction matters for your skin. Most people assume any bar labeled "natural" delivers clean, healthy results. But without knowing what to actually look for, it is easy to end up with a product that strips your skin barrier just as aggressively as a conventional bar would.

This guide covers everything you need to choose wisely: what makes a bar genuinely natural, how to decode an ingredient label, which ingredients work best for your skin type, and how to get the most out of your bar once you have found the right one. By the end, you will be a much smarter soap shopper — and your skin will notice the difference.

What Actually Makes a Soap Bar 'Natural'?

The word "natural" is not regulated on cosmetic labels in the United States. Any brand can print it on a bar without meeting a single defined standard. So the label alone tells you nothing. What matters is the process and the ingredients behind it.

True soap is made through saponification — a chemical reaction between a fat or oil (like coconut oil or olive oil) and an alkali, typically sodium hydroxide, also called lye. Here is the important part: the lye is fully consumed in the reaction. None of it remains in the finished bar. What you get instead is soap molecules, water, and glycerin. For a deeper look at the chemistry, this guide on how soap works breaks it down clearly.

Contrast that with synthetic detergent bars, sometimes called "syndets." These are made from petroleum-derived surfactants and go through no saponification process at all. In fact, they legally cannot be called "soap" in the US — which is why many mass-market bars are labeled "beauty bar" or "cleansing bar" instead. Read the fine print and you will often see them.

One more thing syndets miss: glycerin. Glycerin is a natural by-product of saponification. It is a humectant — meaning it draws moisture toward your skin. Commercial manufacturers frequently extract it from their soap and sell it separately as a cosmetic ingredient. A well-made natural bar keeps it in, which is part of why your skin feels noticeably different after switching.

Key Ingredients in Natural Soap Bars (And What They Do for Your Skin)

Not all natural soap bars are built the same. The base oils and additions a maker chooses shape how a bar feels, how it lathers, and what it does for your specific skin. Here are the most common ingredients worth knowing:

  • Coconut oil: Creates a rich, bubbly lather and has naturally antimicrobial properties. It is one of the most cleansing base oils you can use. The caveat: a very high concentration of coconut oil can be drying for some people, so a well-balanced bar pairs it with more conditioning oils. Real Skin Care's bar is built on saponified organic virgin coconut oil — read more about why in our coconut oil bar soap benefits deep dive.
  • Shea butter: An emollient that adds creaminess to the lather and softens skin. It is especially valued in bars for dry and sensitive skin because it leaves a light conditioning layer after rinsing.
  • Olive oil: A traditional cold-process soap staple. It is high in oleic acid, gentle on skin, and conditioning — though it produces a softer, creamier lather rather than big bubbles.
  • Castor oil: Used in small amounts, it boosts lather and adds humectant properties, helping the bar feel moisturizing rather than stripping.
  • Essential oils: Provide scent without synthetic fragrance. Lavender is calming, tea tree is antibacterial and helpful for oily or blemish-prone skin, and lemongrass is bright and clarifying. Real Skin Care's bar uses all three — organic lavender, tea tree, and lemongrass essential oils. Worth noting: some essential oils (like peppermint or citrus) can irritate very sensitive skin, so fragrance-free options do exist for those who need them.
  • Kaolin clay: A gentle detoxifying addition that draws out impurities without being harsh. Well-suited to oily and combination skin types.
  • Colloidal oatmeal: Finely ground oats suspended in the bar. Soothing and anti-inflammatory, it is a go-to for eczema-prone and reactive skin.

One formulation note: Real Skin Care's natural coconut oil bar contains saponified organic virgin coconut oil plus organic essential oils of lavender, tea tree, and lemongrass. That is it. Four ingredients, fully declared, no hidden components. It is a good example of what ingredient transparency actually looks like in practice.

Natural Soap Bars vs. Commercial Soap — What's Really Different?

The difference is not just philosophical. It shows up on your skin.

Commercial bars — and many "beauty bars" — rely on synthetic surfactants derived from petroleum to do the cleaning. Those surfactants are effective at removing dirt, but they are not selective. They strip your skin's natural oil barrier along with everything else. Your skin then responds by overproducing sebum to compensate, which can leave oily skin oilier and dry skin even more dehydrated.

Natural soap bars, made through cold-process saponification, retain glycerin. That glycerin acts as a humectant — it pulls moisture toward the surface of the skin during and after your wash. The result is skin that feels clean but not tight.

Fragrance is another big difference. Synthetic fragrances in commercial bars are a documented cause of contact dermatitis and allergic reactions. The term "fragrance" or "parfum" on an ingredient label can legally represent a blend of dozens of undisclosed synthetic chemicals. Natural bars use essential oils for scent — or skip fragrance altogether for sensitive skin formulations.

And then there are the extras: preservatives like parabens, chelating agents like EDTA, and artificial colorants are common in commercial formulations but absent from well-made natural bars. Making the switch means fewer synthetic additives touching your skin every single day.

How to Choose the Best Natural Soap Bar for Your Skin Type

There is no single best natural soap bar for everyone. Your skin type shapes what ingredients will work for you and which ones might cause problems. Here is a practical breakdown. And if you want curated picks beyond this guide, we have dedicated resources for men's skin needs and women's skin needs as well.

Natural Soap Bars for Dry Skin

Dry skin needs oils that condition more than they cleanse. Look for bars built on high-oleic oils like olive or avocado oil, plus shea butter for added creaminess. Avoid bars that lean heavily on coconut oil alone, or bars with clay — both can lean drying. After you rinse off, follow up with a good moisturizer while your skin is still slightly damp. Our guide to the best coconut oil body lotions for dry skin and the ultimate moisturizing guide are both worth reading if you want to build a complete routine.

Natural Soap Bars for Sensitive and Eczema-Prone Skin

Keep the ingredient list short. Fragrance-free is almost always the safer call. If a bar does include essential oils, lavender is generally the gentlest option. Colloidal oatmeal is soothing and a great addition for reactive skin. Always patch test a new bar on the inside of your wrist before using it all over. And a clear note: this guide is skincare support, not medical advice — if you are managing persistent eczema, please consult a dermatologist before making changes to your routine. For a gentle coconut-oil-based option worth exploring, see our post on the soothing power of coconut oil bar soap.

Natural Soap Bars for Acne-Prone Skin

Tea tree essential oil is your friend here — it is antibacterial and helps manage the bacteria that contribute to breakouts. Kaolin clay and activated charcoal can help with excess sebum without over-drying. Avoid synthetic fragrance and heavy butters in high concentration. One thing to remember: over-stripping acne-prone skin actually backfires. When your skin barrier is damaged, it produces more oil to compensate — which can worsen breakouts. Even acne-prone skin needs a balanced, not harsh, cleanse. Fragrance-free is often the safer bet here too.

Natural Soap Bars for Oily and Combination Skin

A bar with some coconut oil is perfectly fine for oily skin — the lather is beneficial. Look for bars that include clarifying additions like kaolin clay or tea tree oil. Avoid bars heavy in shea butter or cocoa butter, which can feel occlusive for this skin type. The goal is a thorough clean that does not leave a residue.

How to Read a Natural Soap Bar Label

Ingredient labels on cosmetics use INCI names — that stands for International Nomenclature of Cosmetic Ingredients. These are standardized, internationally recognized terms. They are not meant to confuse you, but they can look intimidating if you are not used to them. Here is what to know.

Ingredients are listed in descending order of concentration. The first ingredient is present in the highest amount. The last few ingredients are often present in very small quantities — things like essential oils or colorants.

A few translations worth memorizing:

  • Sodium Cocoate: Saponified coconut oil — this is the base of most natural coconut oil bars
  • Butyrospermum Parkii Butter: Shea butter
  • Olea Europaea Fruit Oil: Olive oil
  • Lavandula Angustifolia Oil: Lavender essential oil
  • Melaleuca Alternifolia Leaf Oil: Tea tree essential oil
  • Cymbopogon Schoenanthus Oil: Lemongrass essential oil

Now for the red flags. The words "fragrance" or "parfum" on a label can legally mask a blend of dozens of undisclosed synthetic chemicals — even on a bar that calls itself natural. A truly transparent brand lists every ingredient individually with no proprietary blend language hiding synthetic components.

Real Skin Care's bar lists four ingredients, each with its full name: saponified organic virgin coconut oil, organic essential oil of lavender, organic essential oil of tea tree, organic essential oil of lemongrass. That is ingredient transparency in practice.

How to Use a Natural Soap Bar Properly for Best Results

Getting the most from your natural bar is partly about how you use it — and how you store it.

  • Lather in your hands first: Work up a lather in your palms or on a washcloth, then apply it to your skin. Rubbing the bar directly on your skin aggressively wears it down faster and does not give you a better clean.
  • Use lukewarm water: Hot water does open pores, but it also strips oils. Lukewarm is the better call, especially if your skin runs dry or sensitive.
  • Rinse thoroughly: Any residue left on the skin can cause irritation. Take an extra few seconds to make sure everything is rinsed clean.
  • Store it on a draining dish: This is the single most common mistake natural bar soap users make. Natural bars have no synthetic preservatives or hardening agents, so sitting in standing water will dissolve them quickly. A well-draining soap dish extends the life of your bar significantly.
  • Expect a short transition period: When you switch from a commercial bar to a natural one, your skin may take two to four weeks to recalibrate. Your sebum production was likely adjusted around synthetic surfactants. During that window, some people experience a brief adjustment in oil levels or texture. It is normal and it passes. Stick with it.

After cleansing, follow up with a moisturizer to lock in hydration. This is especially important if you have dry skin. Our ultimate guide to moisturizing your skin pairs well with this one.

Frequently Asked Questions About Natural Soap Bars

Q: Are natural soap bars better for your skin than commercial bars?
For most people, yes. Natural bars made through saponification retain glycerin, which supports your skin's moisture barrier. Commercial bars often strip that barrier with synthetic surfactants, leaving skin tight or prone to rebound oiliness. The difference is most noticeable for people with dry, sensitive, or reactive skin.

Q: Can I use a natural soap bar on my face?
Some people do, but it depends on the bar and your skin type. Natural bars are generally gentler than commercial bars, but face skin is more delicate than body skin. A bar with a short, clean ingredient list — especially one that is fragrance-free or uses gentle essential oils like lavender — is more likely to work well on the face. Patch test first and see how your skin responds.

Q: Do natural soap bars expire?
Natural bars do not "expire" the way food does, but they can go rancid over time as the oils oxidize — especially if stored improperly. Most natural bars have a shelf life of one to two years. Store them in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight and use them within that window for best results.

Q: Are natural soap bars safe for eczema?
A fragrance-free, minimal-ingredient natural bar is generally a better option for eczema-prone skin than a synthetic detergent bar. Look for bars with colloidal oatmeal or shea butter and nothing that can trigger a reaction. That said, eczema is a medical condition. This guide is informational — if you have active eczema, consult a dermatologist before making changes to your skincare routine.

Q: What is the difference between handmade soap and natural soap?
Not all handmade soap is natural, and not all natural soap is handmade. "Handmade" refers to how a bar is produced — typically in small batches using the cold-process or hot-process method. "Natural" refers to what is in it. The best bars are both: small-batch made with plant-based, natural ingredients and no synthetic additives.

Q: Do natural soap bars really clean as well as liquid soap?
Yes. Saponification produces genuine soap molecules that are highly effective at lifting dirt and bacteria from the skin. The cleansing mechanism is the same whether the product is a bar or a liquid. Natural bars simply do it without petroleum-derived surfactants, synthetic fragrances, or preservatives that can irritate skin over time.

Putting It All Together

Here are the three things worth taking away from this guide. First, real natural soap is defined by its process and ingredients — saponification, retained glycerin, no synthetic detergents. The word "natural" on a label means nothing without that foundation. Second, the right bar depends on your skin type. Dry skin needs conditioning oils. Oily and acne-prone skin benefits from clarifying ingredients like tea tree and kaolin clay. Sensitive and eczema-prone skin needs a short, fragrance-free ingredient list. Third, reading labels is a skill — and now you have it. INCI names are decipherable, greenwashing signals are identifiable, and ingredient transparency is possible to verify.
